clue.text: Two points I start to get: sharpen weapons, speak carefully.

parts.note: two compass points, west and east
taken as written

indicators.note: the start to a word is its opening letter, so only the head of the next word is used

parts.note: supplies its first letter
to hone a blade is to sharpen it on a stone
swords are bladed weapons

explanation.surface: A duellist gets a couple of points, sharpens the blades, then chooses words with care.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like fencing; the colon hides that every word before 'speak' is a piece of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To weigh one's words is an idiom for choosing them deliberately before saying them.

clue.text: What the testator probably does is carry on business with vigor.

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the idiom for doing a job energetically and willingly

explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is a pun: the will here is the legal document, while the idiom uses will to mean determination.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom meaning to toil eagerly, and literally describes someone handling a testament.

clue.text: One hears it's where campers hang out, very compactly.

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase for an adjective: intense in its sense of highly concentrated, packed tight

indicators.note: what one hears is the spoken form, so the answer is a word pronounced like the campers' phrase

parts.note: campers stay in tents

explanation.surface: Campers crammed together under canvas are living at very close quarters.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: intense is an adjective, and here it stands for being densely concentrated.
explanation.definitionFit: Intense can mean concentrated or extreme in degree, which the setter stretches to being very tightly packed.

clue.text: Sounds "cool," with zero entanglements, to get one under your control.

indicators.note: tells us the pieces are said aloud and run together into one word

parts.note: hip is slang for fashionable or cool
having no ties, no attachments at all

explanation.surface: Someone cool and unattached is out to win somebody over.
explanation.walkthrough: Said quickly, hip-nought-ties runs together as the American spelling of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To hypnotize someone is to put them in a trance where they follow your suggestions.

clue.text: Barely visible.

parts.note: reads as 'only just', but here means wearing nothing, bare
able to be seen, so seen bare

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase normally means faint or hard to see; the setter reads barely as 'in the bare', someone seen without clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: A nude person is unclothed, so is literally on view in a bare state.

clue.text: A rebel at one time.

parts.note: Rebel was the nickname for a Confederate soldier in the American Civil War
in the 1860s, when the South seceded

explanation.walkthrough: A rebel sounds like any insurgent; the clue means a Johnny Reb, a soldier of the breakaway Southern states.
explanation.definitionFit: Confederate soldiers came from the South, so a Rebel of the Civil War era was a Southern American.

clue.text: The lowermost deck, which is otherwise cut off.

parts.note: or introduces an alternative, as otherwise does
to lop is to cut off a branch

explanation.surface: A ship's bottom deck is described as the one that would otherwise be cut off.
explanation.definitionFit: The orlop is the lowest deck of a sailing warship, below the waterline.

clue.text: The infant's rubber toys are just fond relatives to certain Brits.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: rubber ducks for a baby's bath

definitions.text: just fond relatives to certain Brits
definitions.meaning: second meaning: duckie and ducks are affectionate forms of address in parts of England, said to friends and family

explanation.walkthrough: In the English Midlands and North, 'duck' or 'duckie' is an everyday endearment, like 'dear' or 'love'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names little rubber bath ducks and is also a regional English term of endearment.

clue.text: English general and governor of Canada, otherwise sounds like you and I are out of buying.

definitions.text: English general and governor of Canada

indicators.note: when letters are out of a word they have left it, so these two are taken from the word buying

parts.note: taken as written
the letter U is pronounced like the word you
taken as written

explanation.surface: A soldier-governor of Canada whose name suggests the two of us can no longer afford anything.
explanation.walkthrough: Julian Byng commanded the Canadian Corps at Vimy Ridge in 1917 and was Governor General of Canada from 1921 to 1926.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Byng was a British Army general and later the Crown's governor general in Canada.

clue.text: Kind of colored around it, as one did after making an error.

definitions.text: as one did after making an error

indicators.note: it points back to the kind, and the colour word wraps round that

parts.note: red is a colour, so something coloured red
a type is a kind or sort

explanation.surface: A typist blushes at a mistake, the coloured face going with the slip.
explanation.definitionFit: After a typing mistake one keys the text again, which is what retyped describes.

clue.text: Some are said to be so in love!

definitions.text: Some are said to be so in love!

parts.words: Some are said to be so
parts.note: points to a saying: some people are said to be this
completes the proverb 'lucky at cards

explanation.walkthrough: The clue leans on the proverb that someone lucky at cards is unlucky in love; the solver supplies the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb pairs good fortune at gambling with misfortune in romance, so the missing word means ill-fated.

clue.text: Looking for such as dormers at a good price?

definitions.text: Looking for such as dormers at a good price?

parts.note: dormers are the upright glazed openings set into a sloping roof, so this reads as buying such fittings
hints at bargain-hunting, which casual browsing of shop displays suggests

explanation.walkthrough: Taken literally it is shopping for windows such as dormers; the real phrase means gazing at displays without buying.
explanation.definitionFit: Window-shopping is browsing goods in shop displays, usually with no intention of purchasing.

clue.text: See 11
Don't move! You don't like to see business come to one!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the command to stay where you are, as two words

definitions.text: You don't like to see business come to one!
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a halt, as when trade comes to a halt

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is a two-word order; the second is the single noun in the idiom 'come to a halt'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stand still is an order not to move, and a standstill is a complete stop in activity.

clue.text: Something that sends things out with a German form in a chopped-up tree.

indicators.note: one part goes inside the other
a tree that is chopped up is broken into pieces, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
mit is the German word for with

explanation.surface: A wood chipper spits out bits of a felled tree in some German-made shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a German form' is the German version of the word with, not a shape or a document.
explanation.definitionFit: An emitter is a device or source that gives off radiation, light or particles.

clue.text: In charge of the hearth, what many a man wears with a good finish.

indicators.note: the A comes at the finish, after the garment

parts.note: a vest is a garment many men wear, an undershirt or waistcoat
A is the top grade, so it stands for good

explanation.surface: A man at the fireside wears his waistcoat and looks well turned out.
explanation.walkthrough: Vesta was the Roman goddess of the hearth, tended by the Vestal Virgins.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman goddess Vesta presided over the household fire and the hearth.

clue.text: Made legitimate, but made David late, perhaps.

indicators.note: made works here as 'turned into something', so the letters are reworked
signals that the letters given are only one possible arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something was approved, though David was held up in the process.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made' appears twice: the first is part of the definition, the second signals rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: To validate something is to confirm it officially, making it legally or formally acceptable.

clue.text: Sir Andrew has a fever with it, but only on part of the face.

parts.note: an ague is a shivering fever, like malaria
the cheek is part of the face

explanation.surface: A knight is feverish, but the flush shows only on his face.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Andrew Aguecheek is the foolish knight in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Andrew Aguecheek is the comic suitor of Olivia in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night.

clue.text: A girl who has a purpose with a couple of points?

parts.note: an aim is a goal or purpose
two compass points, east and east

explanation.surface: A determined girl has a goal and a pair of points to make.
explanation.definitionFit: Aimee is a female given name, so it stands for one particular girl.

clue.text: Suggests a bad French vocal effort, which could knock you out!

parts.note: mal is French for bad
an aria is a solo song in an opera

explanation.surface: A poor French singer gives a performance so bad it could floor the audience.
explanation.definitionFit: Malaria is a fever disease that can leave a sufferer prostrate, laid low for days.

clue.text: Possibly in the etui they find a necessity with the French.

definitions.text: Possibly in the etui they find

parts.note: a need is something necessary
les is French for the, plural

explanation.surface: A sewing case might hold something essential in French style.
explanation.walkthrough: An etui is a small ornamental case for sewing items such as pins, which crossword setters love.
explanation.definitionFit: An etui is a small case for sewing tools, so slim pointed sewing implements are what it typically holds.

clue.text: Your uncle at the old town–first-class, but an old fighting type!

parts.note: Uncle Sam personifies the United States, so he is every American reader's uncle
Ur is the ancient Sumerian city, the crossword's favourite old town
A1 means first-class; written with an I for the 1

explanation.surface: An American relative in an ancient town turns out to be a first-rate old warrior.
explanation.walkthrough: A1, meaning first-rate, appears in grids as the letters AI.
explanation.definitionFit: The samurai were the hereditary warrior class of feudal Japan.

clue.text: You could perhaps get sore this way–being rather pretty.

definitions.text: You could perhaps get sore this way–being rather pretty.

parts.words: You could perhaps get sore this way
parts.note: a reverse instruction: a flower whose name, made wild, would read sore
the plain sense: a hedgerow flower, attractive to look at

explanation.walkthrough: Take the answer as an instruction: let the letters of the flower run wild and you can get sore. The second half then simply describes the bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: The wild rose, or dog rose, is a pretty pink or white hedgerow flower.

clue.text: See 1
Keepsake–some of which are licensed.

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the following words are used, a run inside them

parts.note: the letters are found across these words

explanation.surface: A souvenir, some of which need a licence to own.
explanation.definitionFit: A relic is an object kept as a memento of the past or of a person.

clue.text: Just like the first man, am I surrounded by a bad cad?

indicators.note: the first pair of words is enclosed by the other letters
a bad version of the word is a broken one, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man asks whether, like Adam, he is beset by a scoundrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Adamic is the adjective from Adam, the first man in Genesis, meaning resembling him.

clue.text: When the outgoing water comes up, go over the material so.

indicators.note: in a down light, coming up means the letters read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: the tide is water that goes out and comes in

explanation.surface: When the ebb tide comes in, someone checks over their stuff.
explanation.definitionFit: To edit is to revise a text, checking it through and correcting it.

clue.text: Didn't she get tired, just sitting on a rock? (According to popular stories, with a bunch of flowers.)

definitions.text: Didn't she get tired, just sitting on a rock?

parts.note: lore is the body of traditional tales and beliefs
a lei is a Hawaiian garland of flowers

explanation.surface: A wry question about a legendary maiden perched on a rock, garlanded with flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lorelei is a Rhine siren of German legend who sat on a rock combing her hair and luring boatmen to their death.
explanation.definitionFit: In German folklore the Lorelei sits on a cliff above the Rhine singing to sailors.

clue.text: What that cleaning powder is supposed to do.

definitions.text: What that cleaning powder is supposed to do.

parts.note: names a washing product, whose own name is built on an old verb
the job such a product is meant to do, which that old verb names

explanation.walkthrough: A detergent takes its name from a rare verb meaning to wipe or cleanse; the clue asks for that verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Deterge is a formal verb meaning to cleanse or wipe away, the root of detergent.

clue.text: The thoughtful insurance man probably did, before anything was signed–but it's a chance well taken.

definitions.text: The thoughtful insurance man probably did, before anything was signed
definitions.meaning: first meaning, taken literally: an underwriter works out the hazard before issuing a policy
second meaning: a gamble entered on with the odds weighed

explanation.walkthrough: Read word by word, the first half describes an insurer weighing up the hazard; the phrase itself means a considered gamble.
explanation.definitionFit: A calculated gamble is one taken after assessing the likely odds and consequences.
